title: Cranial Nerves Atlas
subtitle: Map all twelve cranial nerves from nuclei to skull exits and target organs
altText: Chalkboard-style interactive anatomical illustration for Cranial Nerves Atlas, showing labelled structures and pathway relationships.
learningObjectives: Identify the major components of cranial nerves.
Trace clinically relevant inputs, outputs and connections.
Relate focal dysfunction to plausible neurological and behavioural signs.

sections.explainSimply: Cranial Nerves is a set of connected structures that can be explored layer by layer to understand where it sits and what it does.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: This atlas links the anatomy of cranial nerves to behaviour, cognition, neurological signs and clinically meaningful patterns without reducing complex functions to one structure.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: The cranial nerves should be interpreted through spatial relationships, laterality, vascular supply, pathway continuity and distributed network effects. Focal damage can create both local signs and disconnection syndromes.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Think of it as a layered transit map: structures are stations, tracts are routes, and symptoms depend on which junctions or connections are interrupted.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Recognising plausible neuroanatomical patterns supports better referral, formulation and interpretation of cognitive or behavioural change.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Over-localising a symptom to one structure, or treating an atlas view as diagnostic evidence, can produce false certainty.
sections.clinicalPearl: The only sensory system that reaches cortex without an obligatory thalamic relay.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician can select a structure in the Cranial Nerves Atlas and trace its inputs and outputs before comparing the predicted pattern with examination, imaging and functional assessment.
sections.limitationsCautions: This atlas supports learning and clinical reasoning; it does not replace neurological examination, imaging or specialist interpretation.

anatomy.label: CN I — Olfactory
anatomy.connections: Olfactory epithelium; projects to Olfactory bulb and cortex.
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: The only sensory system that reaches cortex without an obligatory thalamic relay.

anatomy.label: CN II — Optic
anatomy.outputs: Chiasm, tract, LGN and visual cortex
anatomy.connections: Retinal ganglion cells; projects to Chiasm, tract, LGN and visual cortex.
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: Field defects localise lesions along the visual pathway.

anatomy.label: CN III, IV and VI
anatomy.function: Coordinate eye movements and pupil responses
anatomy.connections: Brainstem gaze systems; projects to Extraocular muscles and pupil.
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: Patterns of ophthalmoplegia help localise brainstem, cavernous sinus or orbital disease.

anatomy.label: CN V — Trigeminal
anatomy.outputs: Brainstem nuclei and muscles of mastication
anatomy.connections: Face, cornea, oral cavity; projects to Brainstem nuclei and muscles of mastication.
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: Corneal reflex testing samples both trigeminal and facial pathways.

anatomy.label: CN VII — Facial
anatomy.function: Facial expression, taste, lacrimation and salivation
anatomy.connections: Pons and taste receptors; projects to Facial muscles and glands.
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: Forehead sparing suggests a supranuclear lesion rather than peripheral facial palsy.

anatomy.label: CN VIII — Vestibulocochlear
anatomy.connections: Cochlea and vestibular organs; projects to Pontomedullary nuclei.
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: Peripheral and central vestibular signs require different urgency and interpretation.

anatomy.label: CN IX and X
anatomy.connections: Pharynx, larynx and viscera; projects to Nucleus ambiguus and autonomic nuclei.
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: New bulbar symptoms can signal urgent brainstem or neuromuscular disease.

anatomy.label: CN XI and XII
anatomy.function: Head turning, shoulder elevation and tongue movement
anatomy.connections: Motor nuclei; projects to SCM, trapezius and tongue.
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: Tongue deviation and atrophy help distinguish lower from upper motor pathway lesions.

quiz.question: What is the safest way to use the Cranial Nerves Atlas?
options: As a spatial and network guide alongside clinical evidence
To assume one symptom has one location
quiz.rationale: As a spatial and network guide alongside clinical evidence

quiz.question: Which principle best improves lesion interpretation?
options: Consider location, pathways, laterality and network effects
Assume all people have identical anatomy
quiz.rationale: Consider location, pathways, laterality and network effects

quiz.question: What does selecting a structure reveal?
options: Function, inputs, outputs, connections and clinical relevance
quiz.rationale: Function, inputs, outputs, connections and clinical relevance
